data.title: Oil gains on Iran war worries and short-covering ahead of Thanksgiving holidayÂ
data.description:
[HOUSTON] Oil gained late in trading on Friday (Nov 20) as worries about possible attacks in the US-Israeli war with Iran may be renewed and traders were buying crude ahead of next week’s Thanksgiving holiday, with many traders expected to out of the market for much of next week.

Brent crude futures settled at US$92.57 a barrel, up 59 cents, or 0.64 per cent. US West Texas Intermediate futures for December finished at US$83.98 a barrel, up 77 cents, or 0.93 per cent.

Brent is on track for a near 4 per cent decline for the week and the December WTI contract for a 5 per cent weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. This would be the benchmarks’ third straight week of decline.

“The word around the market is the US military position is robust and on a hair trigger,” said John Kilduff, partner with Again Capital. “Buying ahead of the holiday was also definitely part of it, but not as strong as Iran worries.”

“This week we keep having relatively strong export flows out of the Middle East. There is also a narrative ongoing that as long as people are talking, maybe there’s a deal in the making,” said Aldo Spanjer, commodity strategist at BNP Paribas.

Geopolitical risk could once again drive up prices, said Aldo Spanjer, commodity strategist at BNP Paribas.

“The prices are correct if you believe that this geopolitical risk doesn’t come back. I’m not in that camp who thinks this is done ... I probably see a rebound,” Spanjer said.

On Friday, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement warned workers and people near Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports to evacuate immediately and urged shipping companies to remove vessels, saying they would target Saudi ports in Jeddah and the Red Sea if a Saudi-led coalition strikes Yemen’s Hodeidah port. The Houthis fired missiles at Riyadh on Thursday.

Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and “are burning,” Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by state media on Thursday.

Iran’s intensifying attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, “running at roughly one incident per day in November,” still add a meaningful geopolitical risk premium to the market, according to UOB Group analysts in a client note.

Opec+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on Nov 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia.

The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4 per cent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency said on Thursday.

However, some analysts expect softness in the broader equities markets to weigh on oil prices, as Asian shares fell on Friday — heading for their worst week since 2020.

“Supply disruptions remain a risk, but near-term demand concerns tied to the AI trade unwind and broader risk-off sentiment are weighing on prices,” said Saxo analysts in a note.

In Russia, crude oil output could fall again as Ukrainian attacks on refineries and export infrastructure intensify, analysts and traders say. Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45 per cent since late October, Reuters reported on Wednesday. REUTERS

data.title: European shares post worst week in over a year as AI trade unravels
data.description:
EUROPEAN shares fell 2 per cent on Friday (Nov 20) and marked their steepest weekly decline since late March 2025, as investors unwound AI-linked bets after Anthropic’s blockbuster market debut failed to revive confidence in the sector, deepening a selloff that spread beyond technology stocks.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 closed down 2 per cent to 625.65 points, logging a weekly loss of more than 5.7 per cent, and registered its fifth straight session of declines. The index closed at a six-week low.

Anthropic reached a roughly US$2 trillion valuation in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday after a record IPO raise. But the shares dropped on Friday as the high-profile debut did little to ease concerns about the returns on massive AI spending.

Chip-linked stocks such as ASML and STMicroelectronics shed more than 9 per cent, dragging the tech sector down 5.4 per cent in its steepest one-day fall since October 2025.

The AI trade that has underpinned a global equities rally in recent years came under pressure as investors questioned debt-fuelled spending, while political uncertainty in the US added to concern over the pace of the sector’s expansion.

Investors also worried that a slowdown in AI-related spending could weigh on global economic growth, hurting sectors dependent on economic activity and business investment.

“The amplitude of the technology selloff is threatening the economic outlook and the latter is threatening probably the European cyclical stocks that are not necessarily benefiting from this technology selloff due to this reason, due to the impact that it is going to have on broader economic activity,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior market analyst at Swissquote Bank.

Cyclical sectors including banks, defence and luxury were among the other major laggards down over 2.5 per cent.

“There’s definitely a reassessment of AI and some nervousness around the trade,” said Mark Preskett, senior portfolio manager at Morningstar Wealth in London. “Investors are sitting on good profits, so there’s clearly some profit-taking. Multiples continue to fall for the hyperscalers and especially for semiconductor stocks.”

Among other movers, Abivax plunged 17.2 per cent after Scorpion Capital disclosed a short position in the French biotech firm.

Vallourec tumbled 14.6 per cent after the French steel pipe maker reported a 26 per cent drop in third-quarter core profit, citing the impact of the Iran conflict and operational disruptions in the US.

Despite this week’s losses, the Stoxx 600 is up 5.8 per cent year-to-date, outperforming the S&P 500’s roughly 3 per cent gain and underscoring the resilience of European equities, which recently hit record highs on the back of stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings.

Consumer staples stocks outperformed, with Nestle, Unilever and British American Tobacco up more than 1 per cent each as investors sought refuge in defensive sectors. REUTERS

data.title: US stocks: Wall Street ends sharply lower on AIÂ selloff, S&P 500, Dow in correction
data.description:
[NEW YORK] US stocks extended their rout on Friday (Nov 20), and the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic’s momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year’s stock market rally.

All three major US equity indexes ended sharply lower. The Dow and the S&P 500 are now more than 10 per cent below their record closing highs, confirming both indexes have entered a correction.

The bellwether S&P 500 notched its seventh consecutive drop, its longest losing streak since February 2020.

The S&P 500 and the Dowlogged their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his market-rattling “liberation day” tariff package.

The Nasdaq’s weekly drop was its largest since March 2020. The tech-heavy index hasdipped into negative territory for the year.

“This is clearly a challenging day for capital markets, and as we head into a Friday close, appears to be accelerating to a certain degree,” said Bill Northey, senior investment director at US Bank Wealth Management in Billings, Montana. “But as we step back and evaluate fundamentals and sentiment, sentiment is clearly winning the day today.”

“Sentiment is always the more powerful force in the immediate space, whereas fundamentals tend to win out over time,” Northey added, referring to economic strength and solid corporate earnings, among other things.

Anthropic’s supersized debut as a publicly held company, which was intended to raise as much as US$2 trillion in market cap, failed to catch fire on Thursday, closing 17.1 per cent above its US$83 offer price as enthusiasm for the stock faded throughout the session.

In its second day as a publicly held company, Anthropic’s shares fell 9.1 per cent. Nvidia’s shares tumbled 13.8 per cent.

The Anthropic IPO, combined with Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, failed to dispel fears over risks associated with artificial intelligence and the massive expenditures on the nascent technology.

“Nvidia reported what might have been one of the greatest quarters in corporate earnings history; they did everything right,” said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana. “A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn’t.”

The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has powered much of the broader stock market’s gains in recent months, was up as much as 106.6 per cent in mid-June. That luster has faded, with the index’s year-to-date advance having shrunk to 18.7 per cent.

Among hyperscalers, Amazon fell 3.9%, while Meta dropped 5.9%.

Neocloud firm CoreWeave fell 12.1 per cent and its peer Nebius slid 16.1 per cent.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93 per cent, to 48,147.33, the S&P 500 lost 265.41 points, or 3.7 per cent, to 6,910.42 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261.47 points, or 5.28 per cent, to 22,617.73.

The CBOE Market Volatility Index, often referred to as Wall Street’s “fear gauge,” rose to its highest close since Apr 7, 2025.

Inflation, Fed in focus

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said the central bank’s policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels.

Markets are pricing a near-certain likelihood of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool.

Next week’s personal consumption expenditures (PCE) figures will provide further clarity on the Fed’s monetary policy path after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report last week.

Among other movers, Intuit shares fell 12.8 per cent after the company cut its annual revenue growth forecast and agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about US$3.68 billion, five years after acquiring it for nearly three times as much.

UnitedHealth rose 2.8 per cent after TD Cowen upgraded its shares to a “buy” from a “hold” rating.

The AI selloff also sent Caterpillar 5 per cent lower on worries over weakening demand for its power-generating and backup power equipment.

Cryptocurrency firms including Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood tumbled between 6.3 per cent and 9.6 per cent after bitcoin dropped below the US$60,000 level.

Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.77-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 38 new highs and 1,199 new lows on the NYSE.

On the Nasdaq, 928 stocks rose and 3,964 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 4.27-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 3 new 52-week highs and 28 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 21 new highs and 826 new lows.

Volume on US exchanges was 25.19 billion shares, compared with the 19.50 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: Ask not what AI can do for you
data.description:
I CONFESS I am old-school.

For years, colleagues and friends have regarded me as someone slow to embrace change, particularly technology. This observation is not entirely misplaced.

Yet something unexpected has happened. I find myself taking to artificial intelligence with an enthusiasm that has surprised even me.

More amusingly, some who once considered me technologically challenged have yet to embrace it to the same extent.

I have been reflecting on this irony. Perhaps our ability to benefit from AI has less to do with technological proficiency and more to do with our willingness to learn, the questions we ask and what we choose to do with the answers.

We have spent considerable time asking what AI can do for us. Let’s reframe that question.

Learning begins with wanting to learn

My work in executive education brings me into conversations with leaders and organisations across industries and geographies. I have come to recognise an important distinction: Teaching someone AI is not the same as making that person want to learn AI.

There is a saying that leadership cannot simply be taught; it must also be caught. Something similar may apply to AI.

In the Singapore Management University’s public programmes, participants who self-enrol often arrive with curiosity and questions. In customised corporate programmes, participants may be nominated by their organisations.

Many are enthusiastic, but others have yet to discover why the learning matters to them.

Increasingly, I see greater value in beginning not with the technology, but with a problem. When participants identify a genuine pain point in their work and explore how AI might help them address it, the learning becomes purposeful. The problem belongs to them, along with the desire to solve it.

Organisations can provide access, tools and training. But they cannot mandate curiosity.

The advantage of youth and the value of experience

I marvel at how effortlessly my son, who works in professional services, uses AI to analyse complex data sets, identify patterns and generate insights for his managers. My younger colleagues display the same fluency.

Watching them, I sometimes wonder whether those who developed expertise the hard way have been overtaken.

When a doctoral candidate recently described how AI was accelerating her research, I felt a twinge of envy. My years of doctoral research were difficult, spent poring over papers, wrestling with competing arguments, and enduring frustration, tears and self-doubt.

Yet, that time taught me something invaluable: to question assumptions, recognise inconsistencies and exercise judgment when answers were elusive.

Today, when AI produces convincing responses in seconds, that experience helps me recognise what is missing and ask better questions.

I do not wish those struggles on today’s researchers. Removing drudgery is progress. But removing the intellectual effort through which judgment develops is another matter.

The challenge is to ensure convenience does not replace thinking.

Real magic happens when the digital fluency of the younger generation meets the lived experience and judgment of the older, creating outcomes neither could achieve as effectively alone.

Where empathy makes the difference

Recently, two friends faced deeply distressing circumstances. One lost a life partner. Another was diagnosed with a terminal illness. In both situations, AI proved useful in helping me navigate unfamiliar terrain, gather information and consider ways of supporting their families.

But there were moments when information alone fell short. AI may suggest words of comfort, but it cannot take our place beside a grieving friend.

At the workplace of our terminally ill friend, senior leaders took time to speak with the family, help them navigate complex arrangements and explore ways to ease their financial burden. Colleagues quietly assumed additional responsibilities.

What moved me was the genuine concern that drove these actions. People chose to go beyond their roles because a colleague and their family needed them.

We often speak of empathy as a soft skill, something desirable but perhaps secondary to intelligence and productivity. I argue otherwise.

Empathy makes us pause before acting, consider another person’s circumstances and recognise that the most efficient solution may not always be the most compassionate one.

AI can help organisations make informed decisions, allocate resources and improve efficiency. But human leaders must still decide what matters, whom their decisions affect and when compassion should take precedence over convenience.

Imagine a world where AI enables us to do more in less time, but we become less willing to give that time to one another. What, then, have we really gained?

Technology can expand our capacity to help. Empathy gives that capacity a human purpose.

The question that matters

Much of public discourse about AI centres on whether machines will replace human beings. The concerns are real. Some jobs will change significantly, and some tasks may disappear altogether.

But our preoccupation with replacement may be distracting us from a more immediate responsibility.

Are we becoming better thinkers because of AI, or merely faster producers of answers? Are we using the time it saves to exercise better judgment, deepen relationships and solve meaningful problems?

I am grateful to be living through this transformation at this life stage. The years spent studying, working, making mistakes and learning from people have given me a foundation from which to engage with AI in ways I could not have earlier. I am also learning from younger colleagues who approach it with admirable openness and confidence.

I will probably remain old-school in many ways. But if that means valuing hard-earned knowledge, sound judgment, human relationships and empathy, I am content to carry those qualities into the new world.

AI may help me accomplish more than I ever imagined. But what I choose to do, why it matters and whose lives I touch remain questions that I must answer for myself.

The writer is head of commercial, executive development, at Singapore Management University

data.title: Mercedes GLC 400 electric review: One hidden feature sets it apart from other EVs
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The Mercedes-Benz GLC 400 electric AMG Line Sport has a feature you can’t see, can’t hear and, if its engineers have done their jobs, can’t feel. It’s also what sets it apart from the average electric vehicle.

It’s a two-speed gearbox, and it makes the Mercedes ballistic. With 489 horsepower (hp) on tap, the GLC isn’t exactly under-endowed, but it goes like a cannonball, hurtling violently through space in a way that feels even quicker than its zero-to-100 kmh time of 4.3 seconds suggests.

A high gear helps with range. I was on course for 614 km on a full charge, against Mercedes’ claim of 687 km, and not far off the 622 km I managed in the BMW iX3 50 xDrive M Sport, whose battery is about 15 kWh bigger.

That’s the sort of tech wizardry one likes to see from Mercedes. In fact, the GLC might be built on new-fangled, dedicated, EV underpinnings, but it reminded me of the Benz of old.

Ancient lore holds that engineers once ruled the company, and after doing their thing, they would tell the accountants how much they needed to charge for the cars, instead of the other way around.

In a similar way, the GLC smacks of glorious overkill in places. An enormous, borderless 39.1 inch “Hyperscreen” stretches across the dashboard, turning the interior into a space-age realm of light and colour that is stunning to look at (and relatively straightforward to use).

Another crowd-pleaser: Tap a virtual button and electrochromic tech darkens the glass roof either all at once or in individual sections, foiling the sun’s attempt to bake your head.

And while most EVs have a frunk, the GLC’s is both huge (128 litres) and easily opened: You can press down on the Mercedes logo to unlock it instead of groping for a lever in a footwell, a reminder that a frunk is useful only if it’s easy to get at.

The GLC 400 also comes with four-wheel steering, where the rear wheels turn a few degrees to tighten its turning circle, making this mid-size family crossover as manoeuvrable as a hatchback.

Unlike the Hyperscreen, it’s not something to show off on Instagram, but it’s useful, taking the stress out of U-turns and tight car park spaces.

So far, so Mercedes. Aside from being gorgeous, the interior is also cosseting, with firmly padded seats (with massage function for front passengers) and a generally smooth ride, courtesy of air suspension.

It’s not vast in the back the way some EVs are, but it’s roomy enough to work for a family of tall people. Mercedes seems to have decided that space in the boot is more important than an exceptionally spacious cabin, so the GLC can swallow 570 litres of stuff in the back.

On the move, the GLC 400 is more brutally effective than blissfully engaging. Poise and grip are excellent, and the steering offers more feel than you’d expect, especially in Sport mode, but it lacks the scalpel-like precision of the iX3, and never really eggs the driver on.

You can throw it through a bend and come away impressed by its sheer competence, but you’re unlikely to giggle your way home after, the way you might in a fizzy hot hatch.

I wouldn’t blame Mercedes for that, since it’s hard to make an EV engaging, but all the same, you do come away from the experience wondering if you really want the GLC 400’s performance. The GLC 250 is a good S$67,000 cheaper, after all, and with 354 hp to its name, it’s still lively on the go.

Then again, the best bits of the car listed above – the four-wheel steering, air suspension, borderless Hyperscreen and more – come only with the top-spec AMG Line Sport tested here, which costs S$427,888 with a Certificate Of Entitlement. I haven’t driven the GLC 250, but missing those goodies means it’s likely to feel more ordinary.

In either car, I would like some nicer cabin plastics, and even the priciest variant lacks certain frills, such as a head-up display system, rear air-con controls and even ventilated seats.

Still, the thing buyers want most of all from this electric car is a sense of Mercedesness, and the GLC does deliver. Its giant front grille even recalls the classically upright grilles of Benzes from half a century ago, with their old grid patterns portrayed here by countless LEDs, all laid out precisely. Not everything engineers do has to go unseen, it seems.

data.title: AI can manage a familyâs wealth. It cannot decide what the wealth is for
data.description:
WITHIN a few years, artificial intelligence will take over much of the work in managing family wealth.

Consolidating accounts across entities, checking documents against the law, drafting and monitoring agreements, producing reports on every holding – tasks that occupy accountants, lawyers and family office staff are being automated.

Singapore and Hong Kong, where governments have actively courted family offices, will be among the first places to feel the change.

Consider a typical family that owns three operating companies and a portfolio managed by its single family office in Singapore.

A reporting system pulls figures from all of them every morning. Each company is ahead of budget, and the portfolio is performing better than its benchmark. By every measure on the screen, the year is a success.

Yet, the family has agreed that it will buy out two cousins and that the founder may start a new venture. Neither is communicated to the system; nothing says that the next three years must produce cash to fund these decisions.

Each company owned by the family reinvests its profits, as a well-run company should, and the system reports that this is going well because it was not made aware of new requirements.

The family office uses an investment platform that rebalances the portfolio towards its benchmark. The model finds regional property underweight and adds to it. The family’s largest company is a property developer.

Seen from the portfolio’s perspective, the allocation is balanced. Seen from that of the family, its exposure to one market has just gone up disproportionately.

Then a tax tool optimises the group’s structure. It works from the companies’ figures and assumes, as the companies do, that profits are reinvested. Corporate tax falls.

It does not consider tax on dividends because nothing the tool was given says the owners intend to withdraw cash. The plan is optimal for the companies; it is expensive for the family members when they are hit by their tax bill for taking out cash for the buyout and new venture.

Each answer provided by the system is correct. Each system optimises what it was given: the companies’ budgets, the portfolio’s benchmark, the companies’ tax. Each receives its instructions through a different channel.

None of them knows what the owners need, and the whole infrastructure drifts away from the family’s goals.

Compliance, relational, perspective

One way to see where this gap lies is through what I call “the three functions of ownership”: compliance, relational and perspective.

Compliance ensures all aspects of ownership, such as tax and regulatory rules, abide by the law. The law is codified, so much of this task will be automated by AI.

Relational is what the owners agree among themselves: the direction for their wealth, its limits, who acts on their behalf and what is reported back to them. Drafting and monitoring such agreements will also be largely automated, but the agreement itself remains a decision only the owners can take.

Perspective carries the agreement through. It gives each significant investment and business holding a mandate, assesses the strategy proposed to meet it, takes important decisions back to the family and tracks the results.

It does so with the family’s whole wealth in view, optimising within the limits that compliance sets, and, most importantly, reaches the organisation through one channel: the person leading the wealth on the owners’ behalf.

In the hypothetical family above, the chain breaks between the relational and perspective functions.

The owners have an agreement, but it was not decided and written down in the language of perspective. There is nothing to carry through, so each system optimises against the goals of a company or a portfolio instead.

Decisions still rest with the family

Today, an experienced finance director or family office head who knows what the owners want might catch all three concerns: question the reinvestment plans, notice the added property exposure, ask about dividend tax.

AI can do the same analysis, faster and across every holding, but only if the owners’ requirements have been established. Without that, automation does not close the gap. It makes the gap more consequential.

Closing the chain starts with a clearly communicated agreement. The family decides that they need cash over the next three years for the buy out and the venture, that their investment portfolio should factor in their property company, and that their taxes should be optimised for taking money out.

The person leading the wealth then turns that into instructions every system can work from.

Each company gets a mandate for what it must pay out, so its budget includes the cash the owners need.

The investment platform gets a limit on property allocation for the whole wealth, so owning a property developer does not unbalance the portfolio.

The tax tool is told that cash will be paid out, so dividend tax is part of the plan.

With that in place, AI can do what it does best. It flags the conflicts before the budgets are approved, before the platform rebalances and before the tax plan is adopted. The owners’ time is then spent on the decisions that are theirs.

For advisers, the shift is just as large. Much of what is billed today in compliance and relational work will be done by machines. The value that remains lies in helping owners define what the AI should serve.

AI will make it ever easier to produce information, assess alternatives and carry out decisions. None of that establishes what the wealth is supposed to bring the family. That remains with them, and carrying it through requires a function of its own.

The writer is founder of H S Nielsen, which advises owners of complex wealth structures

The commentary is based on the writer’s own experiences, observations and argument. AI tools were used for drafting in English and editing. The writer remains fully accountable for the commentary’s accuracy, originality and final form.

data.title: Issue 221: COP31 goes big on carbon markets; South-east Asia enhances Asean Power Grid agreement
data.description:
Carbon markets

Policy, aggregation lead carbon approaches at COP31

Public-sector support and market aggregation have emerged as two major areas of focus for carbon markets at the annual United Nations climate conference in Turkey.

South-east Asia, with its rich and abundant ecosystems, stands to gain if governments are able to catalyse improved confidence and scale in carbon markets.

The hosts of the climate meeting, known as COP31, had identified carbon markets as a priority issue to better channel capital towards activities that positively impact climate change.

Over the past week, 17 governments endorsed a “policy playbook” that describes eight levers that policymakers can use to enable carbon credit markets at “speed and scale”. The playbook is authored by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, a group of 18 governments – including Canada, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore and Britain – working to unlock corporate demand for high-integrity carbon credits.

The playbook has a noticeably practical bent, with the policy levers going beyond broad principles to policy actions for countries to implement. The eight levers themselves serve three policy objectives:

  • Support corporate purchases of high-integrity carbon credits;
  • Build buyer confidence and mitigate risk; and
  • Support the development of effective carbon credit markets.

Singapore has also been active on the carbon markets front at COP31.

A Singapore-World Bank partnership known as the Singapore Carbon Markets for Development Programme has released a three-year work plan aimed at helping developing countries to build infrastructure and capabilities to take part in carbon markets.

Singapore authorised the first project aligned with international rules that govern cross-border trading of carbon credits, a clean-water initiative in Rwanda. Preliminary carbon credit deals have also been secured with Kenya and Colombia.

The policy playbook, the cross-border carbon deals and government-driven carbon market initiatives reflect growing government involvement in carbon markets as countries and industries pursue decarbonisation targets, and could provide important tailwinds if supportive policies are put in place.

Another piece of the carbon market puzzle is scale, and aggregation appears to be a favoured solution of the moment.

A Singapore-initiated public-private group called the Action for a Resilient Climate (ARC) coalition – which aims to raise corporate demand for carbon credits – plans to launch its first tender in 2027 to buy a million tonnes of credits.

The policy playbook explains the logic of aggregation. The hypothesis is that pooling demand reduces due diligence costs, supports market building and proofs of concept, and improves the financeability of projects through long-term offtake agreements. Buyers benefit because they can spread risk, improve access and standardise risk management.

Aggregation is being applied on the supply side as well, with project aggregation among the approaches being explored by the Singapore-World Bank programme.

The focus on carbon markets bodes well for South-east Asia, as does the fact that Indonesia, the Philippines and Singapore are part of The Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets. The region continues to face a sizable climate investment gap, which thriving carbon markets can help to close. One estimate by Singapore bank DBS places the region’s cumulative climate investment requirement at US$5.2 trillion from 2025 to 2035 across mitigation, adaptation and resilience areas.

EY notes that South-east Asia accounts for about 30 per cent of the world’s nature-based solutions potential, and has the world’s largest “blue carbon” storage capacity largely due to mangrove areas. Blue carbon projects, in particular, also offer substantial biodiversity benefits. The consultancy estimates that nature-based solutions projects have delivered internal rates of return between 2 and 12 per cent.

A 2025 green-economy report by Bain & Co, GenZero, Google, Standard Chartered and Temasek estimates that South-east Asia’s six largest economies issued about 20 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent credits in 2024, far short of the roughly 720 million tonnes of annual credits from nature-based solutions in those countries.

Singapore, in particular, could potentially reap many benefits. Being an urban, natural resource-limited country, Singapore needs to rely on carbon credits as it progresses towards its climate goals. Furthermore, Singapore has a strategic ambition to be a sustainable finance hub, and thriving carbon markets would be important validation for those plans.

Energy transition

Asean Power Grid is more than a bunch of bilateral deals

South-east Asian leaders have signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding (MOU) on the Asean Power Grid (APG), a regionwide electricity network that was first conceived in 1997 but has made little progress in the 30 years since.

Asean covers 11 countries with very different energy profiles across a vast expanse of land and water, hence difficulty in building a regional power network amid such complexity should not be surprising.

In recent years, Singapore’s pursuit of low-carbon energy imports from its neighbours has fuelled optimism that such imports can spark faster progress on the APG. However, there is a limit to how much Singapore’s energy import projects can advance the APG, because there are fundamental differences between the mostly bilateral, one-way import deals that Singapore is trying to set up and the multilateral, two-way interconnections embodied in the APG’s vision of supporting regional energy resilience.

Some of that complexity is explained in the International Energy Agency’s study into financing the APG. A key observation in the report is that most of the investments in cross-border power projects in South-east Asia have been for one-way power exports, but such investments are insufficient to meet the needs of bi-directional, grid-to-grid projects required by the APG.

Among the APG’s goals are to allow South-east Asian countries to harness complementary energy resources. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ announcement about the latest MOU states that the APG can help to “diversify electricity supplies, improve power system resilience and support renewable energy integration”.

A fee framework that governs how much Singapore will pay for electricity from Indonesia is very different from a two-way agreement that would allow Indonesia to buy electricity from Singapore, much less rules that determine how 11 different countries can trade electricity among themselves. There are also questions involving how capital and operating expenditures related to infrastructure and running the networks should be split, with such decisions taking on a substantially different level of complexity in a multilateral arrangement versus a bilateral one.

The point is that while bilateral deals can help to move progress on the APG forward in certain areas, Asean cannot escape the need to establish a common set of fundamental arrangements across the region as a whole. It will certainly be complicated and challenging, but the struggle will almost certainly be worth it when considering the benefits that a deal could unlock.

data.title: Hermes masters the art of the skeleton watch with three sculptural timepieces
data.description:
H08 Squelette   

INTRODUCED in 2021 as Hermes’ first major modern men’s sports watch collection, the H08 collection features a 39 by 39 mm cushion-shaped case softened by curved edges.

Fashioned in satin-finish titanium for the H08 Squelette, the distinctive case frames the new Hermes H1978 S skeletonised movement. Also crafted in titanium, the automatic movement bears the same shape as the case, fitted here with a hollowed D-shaped rotor.

Whether from the front or back, the H08 Squelette looks sleek and contemporary, the muted grey tones of the case and movement melding into each other. The sight of the exposed twin barrels, which hold up to 60 hours of power reserve, and the gear train peeking out from beneath skeletonised bridges convey technical gravitas.

Meanwhile, legibility is ensured with hour markers, hands and a minute track that make up the top layer of the three-dimensional movement construction.

For a watch collection that oozes casual luxury, the Hermes H08 appears, at first, an unusual choice as a canvas for a skeleton watch.

A skeletonised movement exudes delicate craft, almost at odds with the H08’s sportive elegance and dynamism. Yet, the pairing works in the H08 Squelette – not despite the contrast, but because of it.

Arceau Samarcande

Watch collectors get a double treat with the Arceau Samarcande, a watch that pairs the visual delight of a partially open-worked dial with the aural pleasures of a minute repeater.

Encountering the Arceau Samarcande for the first time, one’s attention is immediately drawn to the horse-shaped window on the right of the dial, which offers a glimpse into the skeletonised automatic H1927 movement that drives the watch. 

While the design suggests a touch of caprice – especially with a strategically placed blue screw that evokes the look of a horse’s eye – the dial is an exacting work of art, crafted using Saint-Louis crystal and capped by sapphire crystal, once on the horse-shaped aperture and again over the entire dial. 

The collection’s iconic case remains a familiar sight. Paying homage to Hermes’ heritage as a Parisian harness and saddle workshop, the Arceau Samarcande’s 38 mm case features asymmetrical lugs that recall a stirrup.

Offered in a choice of three executions, the watch comes in a white gold case with a blue dial, a white gold diamond-set case with a white dial, or a rose gold diamond-set case with a white dial.

Slim d’Hermes Squelette Lune

Svelte, sharp and sophisticated, the Slim d’Hermes collection has long been well-appreciated by boardroom executives who desire a less-is-more approach to their watches.

The Slim d’Hermes Squelette Lune, while still able to slide quietly under a shirt cuff, is made for those who value refinement yet are equally at ease with a wrist accoutrement that commands presence.

The new Slim d’Hermes Squelette Lune models, offered in 39.5 mm platinum or DLC-treated titanium cases, are the latest additions to a family that debuted in 2021.

As before, the watch’s automatic H1953 movement is displayed in its full glory, the skeletonised construction augmented by lovely finishing on the hollowed bridges that show off vital components such as the micro-rotor, barrel, and double-hemisphere moonphase with photorealistic moon discs like framed artworks.

Between the two, the model with DLC-treated titanium case offers a subtler accompaniment with a pared-down black gold dial. The platinum model certainly calls for attention with a royal blue dial that sets off the polished and pristine case.
